investigation.title: Remote Agent Creation Failing Due to Swarm Agent Quota Exhaustion (HTTP 409)
investigation.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) are failing in production with identical HTTP 409 conflict errors indicating the swarm agent quota of 100 has been reached. No new agents can be provisioned until existing agents are deleted or the quota is raised.
investigation.rootCause: The production swarm backend is rejecting all POST /api/agents requests with a 409 "agent quota exceeded: limit is 100" error. The org-level agent quota cap of 100 has been hit, preventing the AURA observability eval from creating a new remote agent. Because agent creation is the prerequisite for every downstream check (state, runtime, chat readiness), all sibling checks fail at the same creation step with the same error before any VM provisioning or readiness assertion can be evaluated.
proof: POST /api/agents returned HTTP 409 with body: {"error":"swarm agent already exists: {\"error\":{\"code\":\"conflict\",\"message\":\"conflict: agent quota exceeded: limit is 100\"}}","code":"conflict","details":null} at 2026-06-14T03:48:29.848Z

All three sibling checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) carry the identical 409 error message, confirming the failure is at the shared agent-creation step, not in downstream VM or runtime logic.

The evidence object is empty ({}) for all three checks, meaning no orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, or remoteState was captured — consistent with the request being rejected before any agent resource was allocated.
Latency for all three failing requests is low (1610 ms, 1280 ms, 1586 ms), indicating an immediate server-side rejection rather than a timeout or infrastructure hang.
The inner swarm error code is 'conflict' and the message explicitly states 'limit is 100', confirming this is a hard quota enforcement, not a transient race condition or duplicate-name collision.
possibleCauses: [Most likely] The production org has accumulated 100 swarm agents (the enforced hard limit) and none have been cleaned up, leaving no capacity for the eval's agent creation request.
[Likely] A previous AURA eval run or automated process created agents that were never deleted (e.g., due to a teardown failure), causing agents to accumulate over time until the quota was exhausted.

[Possible] The quota limit of 100 is too low for the current scale of production usage plus observability eval overhead, and the limit needs to be raised at the swarm backend or per-org configuration.
[Less likely] A misconfiguration caused the eval to target an org that is shared with production workloads, meaning real user agents are consuming quota that the eval expects to be available.
[Unlikely] A swarm backend bug is incorrectly counting agents toward the quota (e.g., counting soft-deleted or terminated agents as active).

reproductionSteps.details: If the response returns 100 agents or the total count equals the quota, quota exhaustion is confirmed.

reproductionSteps.details: Expect HTTP 409 with error code 'conflict' and message 'agent quota exceeded: limit is 100'.

reproductionSteps.details: Filter the agent list for agents created by the AURA observability eval (e.g., by name prefix or tag) and check whether they were properly deleted after previous runs.

investigation.title: Remote Agents Blocked by Swarm Agent Quota Exhaustion (HTTP 409 Conflict)
investigation.summary: All three remote-agent checks (create, state, runtime) are failing simultaneously with HTTP 409 responses indicating the swarm agent quota of 100 has been reached. No new agents can be provisioned in the production environment until existing agents are deleted or the quota is raised.
investigation.rootCause: The production swarm backend has reached its hard agent quota limit of 100. Every attempt to POST /api/agents returns a 409 Conflict with the nested error "conflict: agent quota exceeded: limit is 100", preventing the AURA observability eval from creating a test agent and completing any downstream state or runtime checks. This is a capacity/resource exhaustion condition, not a code defect in the eval itself.
proof: All three sibling checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) return identical HTTP 409 responses: {"error":"swarm agent already exists: {\"error\":{\"code\":\"conflict\",\"message\":\"conflict: agent quota exceeded: limit is 100\"}}","code":"conflict","details":null}

The outer error message 'swarm agent already exists' combined with the inner message 'agent quota exceeded: limit is 100' confirms the swarm layer is rejecting creation because the tenant or global agent count is at its ceiling of 100.
All three checks failed within the same 3-second window (03:48:31–03:48:34 UTC on 2026-06-14), indicating a persistent quota-exhausted state rather than a transient race condition.

Evidence payloads for all three checks are empty ({}), confirming no agent was ever successfully created and no downstream state data (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) could be collected — directly violating the expectedOutputContract.

Latencies for all three checks (1280 ms, 1610 ms, 1586 ms) are well within the warningLatencyMs threshold (5000 ms), ruling out a timeout or latency-related failure; the rejection is immediate and deterministic.
possibleCauses: [Highest confidence] Production swarm quota is genuinely exhausted: 100 live agents exist and none have been cleaned up, either because prior eval runs or user workloads created agents that were never deleted, or because a cleanup/teardown step is broken or missing.
[Medium confidence] AURA eval teardown is not deleting its own test agents after each run, causing eval-created agents to accumulate over time until the quota ceiling is hit.
[Medium confidence] A separate production workload or automated process has consumed all 100 agent slots independently of the eval, leaving no headroom for observability checks.
[Low confidence] The quota limit of 100 is misconfigured or too low for the current scale of the production environment, making exhaustion inevitable under normal load.
[Low confidence] The swarm backend is misreporting quota state due to a stale counter or cache, returning 409 even though fewer than 100 agents are actually active.

investigation.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed simultaneously at 2026-06-14T03:48Z with identical HTTP 409 conflict errors indicating the swarm agent quota of 100 has been reached. Because agent creation is a prerequisite for all downstream checks, no check in the remote-agents feature could produce the expected "hello from aura" response evidence.
investigation.rootCause: The swarm backend rejected POST /api/agents with a hard quota limit error ("agent quota exceeded: limit is 100"), preventing the AURA observability eval from provisioning a new test agent. This is a resource exhaustion condition at the swarm layer, not a transient network or application code failure. All three sibling checks share the same failure message and error code, confirming the quota wall is the single upstream blocker for the entire remote-agents feature check suite.
proof: All three checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) returned HTTP 409 with identical error body: {"error":"swarm agent already exists: {\"error\":{\"code\":\"conflict\",\"message\":\"conflict: agent quota exceeded: limit is 100\"}}","code":"conflict","details":null}
The inner swarm error explicitly states: 'agent quota exceeded: limit is 100', confirming a hard ceiling of 100 agents has been reached in the production swarm.

remote-agent-create failed at 03:48:31.458Z, remote-agent-state at 03:48:32.738Z, and remote-agent-runtime at 03:48:34.324Z — all within a 3-second window, indicating a persistent quota state rather than a momentary spike.
No evidence fields were populated in any of the three checks (evidence: {}), confirming zero successful agent provisioning occurred during the eval run.

The expectedOutputContract required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, model, provider, message) and an assertion that message contains 'hello from aura' — none of these could be satisfied because agent creation never succeeded.
possibleCauses: [HIGHEST] Production swarm has accumulated 100 live agents and the hard quota ceiling is enforced synchronously on POST /api/agents, blocking all new provisioning including AURA observability eval agents.
[HIGH] AURA observability eval agents from previous runs were not cleaned up (deleted) after their check cycles completed, causing quota to accumulate over time until the ceiling was hit.
[MEDIUM] A separate workload or automated process provisioned a large number of agents in the same org/namespace, consuming quota that the observability eval depends on.

[LOW] The quota limit of 100 is a per-org or per-environment ceiling that is too low for the combined load of production agents plus observability eval agents, requiring a quota increase rather than a cleanup.

investigation.title: Image Generation Stream Fails with SESSION_OPEN_FAILED (404) — Agent Runtime Harness Unreachable
investigation.summary: The image generation stream check failed immediately after emitting a `generation_start` frame because the agent runtime returned a 404, causing a `SESSION_OPEN_FAILED` error before any progress frames or completion artifacts could be produced. Both required evidence fields (`frameTypes` and `imageUrlPresent`) are absent, confirming the stream never progressed past session initialization.
investigation.rootCause: The agent runtime harness is unreachable at the configured endpoint (LOCAL_HARNESS_URL / SWARM_BASE_URL). The HTTP 404 response during session open indicates either the harness process is not running, the deployment is missing or misconfigured, or the harness version deployed does not expose the expected session-open route. The stream aborted at the very first network call — no generation frames, progress frames, or artifact URLs were ever emitted.
proof: Frame 2 event=generation_error, code=SESSION_OPEN_FAILED: 'agent runtime endpoint not found (404): the harness is unreachable or running an incompatible version.'
Only one meaningful frame was received (generation_start); the stream never emitted generation_completed or any image artifact frame.
Required evidence fields frameTypes and imageUrlPresent are both missing from the eval result.
Check latencyMs=2031ms — well under the warningLatencyMs threshold of 180000ms — confirming the failure was an immediate hard error, not a timeout.
Frame 3 is a bare message event with data=null and raw='', indicating the stream closed abnormally with no payload after the error.
The error message explicitly instructs: 'Verify the harness deployment and the LOCAL_HARNESS_URL / SWARM_BASE_URL configuration.'
possibleCauses: 1. (Highest confidence) The agent runtime harness process is not running or was never deployed to the target environment — the 404 is returned by an upstream router or load balancer with no backing service.
2. (High confidence) LOCAL_HARNESS_URL or SWARM_BASE_URL is misconfigured — pointing to a stale, incorrect, or environment-specific URL that no longer resolves to a live harness instance.
3. (Medium confidence) The harness was deployed but at an incompatible version that does not register the session-open route, causing the 404 at the route level rather than the host level.
4. (Lower confidence) A recent infrastructure change (e.g., namespace migration, ingress rule update, or service rename) broke the route without updating the harness URL configuration.
5. (Lower confidence) The harness is healthy but behind an auth layer or network policy that rejects the eval runner's request as a 404 rather than a 401/403.

investigations.title: Image Generation Stream Fails with SESSION_OPEN_FAILED (404) — Agent Runtime Harness Unreachable
investigations.summary: The image generation stream check failed immediately after emitting a `generation_start` frame because the agent runtime returned a 404, causing a `SESSION_OPEN_FAILED` error before any progress frames or completion artifacts could be produced. Both required evidence fields (`frameTypes` and `imageUrlPresent`) are absent, confirming the stream never progressed past session initialization.
investigations.rootCause: The agent runtime harness is unreachable at the configured endpoint (LOCAL_HARNESS_URL / SWARM_BASE_URL). The HTTP 404 response during session open indicates either the harness process is not running, the deployment is missing or misconfigured, or the harness version deployed does not expose the expected session-open route. The stream aborted at the very first network call — no generation frames, progress frames, or artifact URLs were ever emitted.
proof: Frame 2 event=generation_error, code=SESSION_OPEN_FAILED: 'agent runtime endpoint not found (404): the harness is unreachable or running an incompatible version.'
Only one meaningful frame was received (generation_start); the stream never emitted generation_completed or any image artifact frame.
Required evidence fields frameTypes and imageUrlPresent are both missing from the eval result.
Check latencyMs=2031ms — well under the warningLatencyMs threshold of 180000ms — confirming the failure was an immediate hard error, not a timeout.
Frame 3 is a bare message event with data=null and raw='', indicating the stream closed abnormally with no payload after the error.
The error message explicitly instructs: 'Verify the harness deployment and the LOCAL_HARNESS_URL / SWARM_BASE_URL configuration.'
possibleCauses: 1. (Highest confidence) The agent runtime harness process is not running or was never deployed to the target environment — the 404 is returned by an upstream router or load balancer with no backing service.
2. (High confidence) LOCAL_HARNESS_URL or SWARM_BASE_URL is misconfigured — pointing to a stale, incorrect, or environment-specific URL that no longer resolves to a live harness instance.
3. (Medium confidence) The harness was deployed but at an incompatible version that does not register the session-open route, causing the 404 at the route level rather than the host level.
4. (Lower confidence) A recent infrastructure change (e.g., namespace migration, ingress rule update, or service rename) broke the route without updating the harness URL configuration.
5. (Lower confidence) The harness is healthy but behind an auth layer or network policy that rejects the eval runner's request as a 404 rather than a 401/403.

investigations.title: Remote Agent Creation Failing Due to Swarm Agent Quota Exhaustion (HTTP 409)
investigations.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) are failing in production with identical HTTP 409 conflict errors indicating the swarm agent quota of 100 has been reached. No new agents can be provisioned until existing agents are deleted or the quota is raised.
investigations.rootCause: The production swarm backend is rejecting all POST /api/agents requests with a 409 "agent quota exceeded: limit is 100" error. The org-level agent quota cap of 100 has been hit, preventing the AURA observability eval from creating a new remote agent. Because agent creation is the prerequisite for every downstream check (state, runtime, chat readiness), all sibling checks fail at the same creation step with the same error before any VM provisioning or readiness assertion can be evaluated.
proof: POST /api/agents returned HTTP 409 with body: {"error":"swarm agent already exists: {\"error\":{\"code\":\"conflict\",\"message\":\"conflict: agent quota exceeded: limit is 100\"}}","code":"conflict","details":null} at 2026-06-14T03:48:29.848Z

All three sibling checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) carry the identical 409 error message, confirming the failure is at the shared agent-creation step, not in downstream VM or runtime logic.

The evidence object is empty ({}) for all three checks, meaning no orgId, agentId, vmIdPresent, or remoteState was captured — consistent with the request being rejected before any agent resource was allocated.
Latency for all three failing requests is low (1610 ms, 1280 ms, 1586 ms), indicating an immediate server-side rejection rather than a timeout or infrastructure hang.
The inner swarm error code is 'conflict' and the message explicitly states 'limit is 100', confirming this is a hard quota enforcement, not a transient race condition or duplicate-name collision.
possibleCauses: [Most likely] The production org has accumulated 100 swarm agents (the enforced hard limit) and none have been cleaned up, leaving no capacity for the eval's agent creation request.
[Likely] A previous AURA eval run or automated process created agents that were never deleted (e.g., due to a teardown failure), causing agents to accumulate over time until the quota was exhausted.

[Possible] The quota limit of 100 is too low for the current scale of production usage plus observability eval overhead, and the limit needs to be raised at the swarm backend or per-org configuration.
[Less likely] A misconfiguration caused the eval to target an org that is shared with production workloads, meaning real user agents are consuming quota that the eval expects to be available.
[Unlikely] A swarm backend bug is incorrectly counting agents toward the quota (e.g., counting soft-deleted or terminated agents as active).

reproductionSteps.label: List all current agents for the affected org to confirm quota saturation
reproductionSteps.command: GET /api/agents?limit=100 (with production org credentials) and count returned agents
reproductionSteps.details: If the response returns 100 agents or the total count equals the quota, quota exhaustion is confirmed.

reproductionSteps.details: Filter the agent list for agents created by the AURA observability eval (e.g., by name prefix or tag) and check whether they were properly deleted after previous runs.

reproductionSteps.label: Inspect eval teardown logic for agent deletion
reproductionSteps.details: Review the eval runner's cleanup phase to determine whether DELETE /api/agents/{agentId} is called after each eval run, and whether failures in that call are surfaced or silently swallowed.

reproductionSteps.label: Verify the quota limit configuration in the swarm backend
reproductionSteps.details: Check the swarm backend's org-level quota configuration to confirm the limit is 100 and whether it is configurable per org or globally enforced.

investigations.title: Remote Agents Blocked by Swarm Agent Quota Exhaustion (HTTP 409 Conflict)
investigations.summary: All three remote-agent checks (create, state, runtime) are failing simultaneously with HTTP 409 responses indicating the swarm agent quota of 100 has been reached. No new agents can be provisioned in the production environment until existing agents are deleted or the quota is raised.
investigations.rootCause: The production swarm backend has reached its hard agent quota limit of 100. Every attempt to POST /api/agents returns a 409 Conflict with the nested error "conflict: agent quota exceeded: limit is 100", preventing the AURA observability eval from creating a test agent and completing any downstream state or runtime checks. This is a capacity/resource exhaustion condition, not a code defect in the eval itself.
proof: All three sibling checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) return identical HTTP 409 responses: {"error":"swarm agent already exists: {\"error\":{\"code\":\"conflict\",\"message\":\"conflict: agent quota exceeded: limit is 100\"}}","code":"conflict","details":null}

The outer error message 'swarm agent already exists' combined with the inner message 'agent quota exceeded: limit is 100' confirms the swarm layer is rejecting creation because the tenant or global agent count is at its ceiling of 100.
All three checks failed within the same 3-second window (03:48:31–03:48:34 UTC on 2026-06-14), indicating a persistent quota-exhausted state rather than a transient race condition.

Evidence payloads for all three checks are empty ({}), confirming no agent was ever successfully created and no downstream state data (orgId, agentId, readyState, state) could be collected — directly violating the expectedOutputContract.

Latencies for all three checks (1280 ms, 1610 ms, 1586 ms) are well within the warningLatencyMs threshold (5000 ms), ruling out a timeout or latency-related failure; the rejection is immediate and deterministic.
possibleCauses: [Highest confidence] Production swarm quota is genuinely exhausted: 100 live agents exist and none have been cleaned up, either because prior eval runs or user workloads created agents that were never deleted, or because a cleanup/teardown step is broken or missing.
[Medium confidence] AURA eval teardown is not deleting its own test agents after each run, causing eval-created agents to accumulate over time until the quota ceiling is hit.
[Medium confidence] A separate production workload or automated process has consumed all 100 agent slots independently of the eval, leaving no headroom for observability checks.
[Low confidence] The quota limit of 100 is misconfigured or too low for the current scale of the production environment, making exhaustion inevitable under normal load.
[Low confidence] The swarm backend is misreporting quota state due to a stale counter or cache, returning 409 even though fewer than 100 agents are actually active.

Check for stale or orphaned agents that should have been cleaned up by prior eval runs or user sessions

investigations.summary: All three remote-agent checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) failed simultaneously at 2026-06-14T03:48Z with identical HTTP 409 conflict errors indicating the swarm agent quota of 100 has been reached. Because agent creation is a prerequisite for all downstream checks, no check in the remote-agents feature could produce the expected "hello from aura" response evidence.
investigations.rootCause: The swarm backend rejected POST /api/agents with a hard quota limit error ("agent quota exceeded: limit is 100"), preventing the AURA observability eval from provisioning a new test agent. This is a resource exhaustion condition at the swarm layer, not a transient network or application code failure. All three sibling checks share the same failure message and error code, confirming the quota wall is the single upstream blocker for the entire remote-agents feature check suite.
proof: All three checks (remote-agent-create, remote-agent-state, remote-agent-runtime) returned HTTP 409 with identical error body: {"error":"swarm agent already exists: {\"error\":{\"code\":\"conflict\",\"message\":\"conflict: agent quota exceeded: limit is 100\"}}","code":"conflict","details":null}
The inner swarm error explicitly states: 'agent quota exceeded: limit is 100', confirming a hard ceiling of 100 agents has been reached in the production swarm.

remote-agent-create failed at 03:48:31.458Z, remote-agent-state at 03:48:32.738Z, and remote-agent-runtime at 03:48:34.324Z — all within a 3-second window, indicating a persistent quota state rather than a momentary spike.
No evidence fields were populated in any of the three checks (evidence: {}), confirming zero successful agent provisioning occurred during the eval run.

The expectedOutputContract required evidence fields (orgId, agentId, model, provider, message) and an assertion that message contains 'hello from aura' — none of these could be satisfied because agent creation never succeeded.
possibleCauses: [HIGHEST] Production swarm has accumulated 100 live agents and the hard quota ceiling is enforced synchronously on POST /api/agents, blocking all new provisioning including AURA observability eval agents.
[HIGH] AURA observability eval agents from previous runs were not cleaned up (deleted) after their check cycles completed, causing quota to accumulate over time until the ceiling was hit.
[MEDIUM] A separate workload or automated process provisioned a large number of agents in the same org/namespace, consuming quota that the observability eval depends on.

[LOW] The quota limit of 100 is a per-org or per-environment ceiling that is too low for the combined load of production agents plus observability eval agents, requiring a quota increase rather than a cleanup.
